text: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) targets low loss throughout a weight neighborhood, with weight regularization, rather than at a single parameter setting. A PAC-Bayesian bound connects population loss to worst-case neighborhood training loss and a norm penalty, assuming Gaussian perturbations do not reduce population loss on average and L2 weight norm is at least one; it motivates, but does not certify, the minibatch implementation. SAM approximates the worst-case perturbation using the training gradient, then updates from the gradient at perturbed weights, omitting second-order terms and requiring two backpropagations. Across CIFAR-10/100 configurations, SAM improves over baselines allowed up to twice as many epochs; AutoAugment WideResNet error falls from 2.2% to 1.6% on CIFAR-10, supporting benefits beyond longer pointwise-loss training. Gains extend to ImageNet and EfficientNet finetuning, including 0.30% CIFAR-10 error with ImageNet-plus-JFT-pretrained EfficientNet-L2. Lower Hessian curvature supports the neighborhood-loss rationale. Independent subset perturbations change the effective objective; smaller subsets improve SAM generalization and m-sharpness's predictive value for generalization gaps in the studied settings. Under random label corruption, clean-test accuracy improves, although SAM trails MentorMix and bootstrapping still leaves a deficit at the highest noise rate. One augmented SVHN configuration worsens.

Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) addresses training minima with similar losses but different test performance by optimizing the worst training loss within a parameter neighborhood. A conditional PAC-Bayesian bound motivates the objective, assuming Gaussian weight perturbations do not lower population loss and Euclidean weight norm is at least one, without certifying approximate minibatch updates. The practical optimizer uses one gradient to choose a loss-increasing perturbation and another at perturbed weights to update the original parameters. Across tested CIFAR configurations, SAM improves generalization even when non-SAM baselines can train for twice as many epochs, supporting a benefit beyond longer point-loss optimization. Lower measured Hessian curvature in the tested model also supports the intended neighborhood geometry. Gains extend to ImageNet ResNets and EfficientNet finetuning after ImageNet or ImageNet-plus-JFT pretraining. Under random label noise, unbootstrapped SAM improves clean-test accuracy over SGD but trails reported MentorMix results; one augmented SVHN configuration regresses. A complementary analysis evaluates sharpness through separate loss maximizations on subsets, defining m-sharpness. Smaller subsets improve generalization in the studied training setting and predict generalization gaps better than full-training-set sharpness.

VoxPoser translates language-specified manipulation subtasks into spatial objectives, allowing motion planning to combine desired motions and avoidance constraints rather than relying on sequential action primitives. Language-model-generated programs query visual perception and assign values to three-dimensional locations for an end-effector, object, or object part; planners optimize trajectories against these maps and replan from observations without additional training. Across five real-world tabletop tasks, success reaches 88% in static scenes and 70% under disturbances, versus 24% and 0% for an LLM using simple primitives. This comparison supports spatially composed objectives as an executable alternative to direct primitive parameterization, including when observations change. Across 13 simulated tasks, category averages favor VoxPoser on seen and unseen instruction/attribute splits, although individual tasks sometimes favor baselines. For contact-rich tasks, synthesized trajectories additionally focus exploration near task-relevant interactions for online dynamics learning. On three simulated tasks, this raises success from 3.3-18.3% zero-shot to 80.0-91.7%, with mean interaction times below three minutes, whereas learning without priors exceeds 12 hours. Thus, trajectories insufficient for zero-shot completion can still guide adaptation; perception errors, restricted environment dynamics, and end-effector-only planning delimit the demonstrated scope.

VoxPoser turns language-specified manipulation subtasks into spatial objectives, allowing motion planning to satisfy affordances and constraints jointly rather than sequence predefined actions. Pretrained language models generate programs that query visual perception and compose three-dimensional voxel maps; planners optimize trajectories against these maps and replan from updated observations without additional training. Across five tabletop robot tasks, success averages 88% without disturbances and 70% with disturbances, versus 24% and 0% for a language-model-plus-primitives baseline. This comparison supports spatial composition as an alternative to primitive sequencing for these tasks, including disturbed execution. Category-level gains over that baseline and learned costmaps on 13 simulated tasks support transfer to unseen instructions and attributes, but task-level improvements are uneven. For contact-intensive simulated door, window, and fridge tasks, zero-shot trajectories alone are insufficient; using them as exploration priors concentrates action sampling near relevant interactions. Dynamics learning then takes under three minutes of online interaction, whereas exploration without priors exceeds a twelve-hour limit, supporting the trajectories' additional role in guiding learning for contact-intensive tasks. The approach depends on manually supplied prompt examples and perception, and its implementation plans end-effector rather than whole-arm trajectories.
